concerns: Manufacturability & yield: bounded/fractionated small-EV peaks may provide very low biomass per lot; insufficient yield will impair parallel orthogonal analytics and reproducibility assessments across >=3 lots.

Process sensitivity & buffer/device compatibility: capture reagents and spike-in tracer may be incompatible with mucin mimics or device rinse buffers, causing false negatives/positives unless prequalified in the exact matrix.

Measurement feasibility & reproducibility: intact immuno-capture + spike-in detection and downstream detergent/protease protection assays are technically demanding at low particle counts; particle counting, capture ELISA, and functional assays must be validated for low-biomass precision and limits of detection before relying on pass/fail gating.

Secretome/mucin confounding: mucin- or excipient-stabilized soluble complexes could mimic membrane protection under protease/detergent conditions, producing false-positive protected activity unless additional orthogonal controls are included (e.g., density behavior, multiple capture markers, enzymatic digestion panels).

Lot comparability & stability: adopting a qualitative protected-fraction gate shifts comparability risk onto early lot-to-lot variability of capture recovery and bioassay readout; without defined numeric stability/acceptance criteria, passing lots may still vary during scale-up or storage.

Scale-up risk: if the protected-fraction is a rare subpopulation, scale-up runs may fail to reproduce protected recovery or functional signal, requiring alternate source-cell expansion, concentration/fractionation changes, or a pivot to secretome-centric definitions.

Quality-attribute relevance & regulatory risk: the proposed qualitative gate is defensible for early selection but leaves open how to translate to releaseable potency/identity attributes; regulators may request quantitative, stability-qualified assays before permitting bridging or clinical comparability studies.
conclusion: The proposed spike-in–controlled, fraction-level protected-bioactivity experiment is conceptually aligned with current EV quality guidance and with rodent intranasal efficacy reports; it is an appropriate, discriminating early CMC gate to determine whether an EV-enriched bounded fraction (after simulated device/mucin exposure) carries membrane-protected activity distinct from secretome. However, practical manufacturability and translational risks are substantial: the approach is highly assay- and reagent-dependent, sensitive to low-biomass yield and buffer/device incompatibilities, and even a positive protected in vitro signal would not guarantee non-human-primate or human delivery. Proceeding with the experiment is recommended only after prequalification of spike-in tracer and capture reagents, demonstration of sufficient per-lot material yield, and explicit criteria for how a qualitative pass/fail will affect downstream scaling and bridging decisions.
evidence_gap: No direct evidence that protected-fraction in vitro bioactivity after device/mucin passage predicts large-animal (NHP) or clinical intranasal brain delivery; limited published information about assay sensitivity and reproducibility for low-biomass capture/functional readouts in clinical-device matrices.
